The most suitable counties gain between 5 and 10% of additional suitable land, with the exception of Prairie County, which is supplanted by Teton County at 72.9% suitability. Looking now to the siting results for a dry-cooled SMR in Table M3, it seems the eastern half of the state opens up significantly for potential suitable land, primarily due to the removal of the cooling water requirement. One exception lies in Roosevelt County, which is almost entirely occupied by the Fort Peck Indian Reservation. Similarly, the Crow and Northern Cheyenne Reservations preclude most of Big Horn County. These instances aside, the removal of the cooling water requirement means that 32 Montana counties have greater than 50% suitability, with 8 of those reaching 90% or more. Given the significantly relaxed siting criteria for data center technology, it is little surprise that Table M4 shows most of the state as suitable, with the notable exception of Mineral County, which finds itself tucked into one of the most topologically diverse regions in the state. What is less evident is the rationale behind the locations of existing fiber optic lines and data centers when so much of the state should be suitable. While there are no apparent missing criteria, the siting parameters do not account for incentives. In this case, most of the major fiber optic intersections and some data center locations coincide with the major population centers of Billings, Boseman, Helena, and Missoula. The impact of this phenomenon on the opportunities for collocation can be seen in Table M5, which shows that the primary intersection of available fiber optic networks with potential locations for nuclear power are in the southeast quadrant of the state surrounding the Yellowstone River.
